FAST

Nov 25 : AI-linked stocks extended their slide in premarket trading on Wednesday, with chipmakers, server makers and data center operators all falling as investors weighed the soaring cost of the AI infrastructure buildout against its returns. Investors have set a high bar for AI-linked companies, punishing shortfalls and offering little reward for beating expectations and raising outlooks, as concerns grow over heavy, often debt-fueled infrastructure spending and uncertain returns. Dell Technologies slumped 7.2 per cent on Wednesday despite the server maker raising its annual revenue and profit forecasts for the third time this year and approving an additional $25 billion share buyback. "Investors are focused on the big and rising cost of building AI, so good earnings and impressive earnings forecasts no longer lift sentiment," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote Bank.

Rival AI server maker HPE tumbled 16.3 per cent on Tuesday after raising its full-year revenue outlook. Its shares and those of rival Super Micro declined 5.2 per cent and 3.6 per cent, respectively, on Wednesday. Shares of Ambarella, valued at $2 billion, tumbled 36 per cent after the AI semiconductor firm forecast fourth-quarter revenue below analysts' estimates. Nvidia, which has been at the heart of the turmoil, fell 4.6 per cent, extending Tuesday's 6 per cent slide, as the rally sparked by CEO Jensen Huang's rehiring quickly lost steam. Anthropic dropped 5.6 per cent, trading well below its $83 initial public offering price just days after the Claude developer's record-breaking Nasdaq debut. DEBT STRAIN Neocloud providers, which rent out specialized AI computing capacity, have been under pressure since October over concerns about the debt funding their rapid expansion. The Democrats' victory in the midterm elections this month has added to those worries, with investors weighing the prospect of a data center slowdown from tougher AI regulation and more hurdles to construction. Nvidia-backed neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius Group each fell about 6 per cent, while IREN, Applied Digital and Core Scientific lost more than 4 per cent. The yield on CoreWeave's bonds due 2031 rose to almost 18 per cent as prices fell more than 1.6 cents on the dollar to near record lows, Tradeweb data showed. The cost of insurance against tech companies defaulting on debts has jumped sharply, with five-year CDS spreads at Oracle, Alphabet, SpaceX and CoreWeave hitting record levels. Shares of AI hyperscalers were broadly lower, with Oracle, Alphabet, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms and Microsoft down between 1.4 per cent and 4.3 per cent.

Source: Reuters

FAST

MUMBAI, Nov 25 : Indian fintech PhonePe has resumed preparations for its initial public offering and is targeting a listing in the first three months of next year at a valuation of $12 billion to $15 billion, a person directly aware of the discussions said. The Walmart-backed company is expected to file its updated draft papers with India's market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, within the next 30 to 45 days, the person said, requesting anonymity as talks are confidential. The listing is set to be India's biggest fintech debut since Paytm's $2.5 billion float in 2021. PhonePe had paused its listing plans in March due to global capital market volatility stoked by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The issue will be an entirely secondary share sale to raise $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion, retaining the size outlined in PhonePe's January draft prospectus, where majority owner Walmart said it would trim its stake by about 12 per cent, and investors Tiger Global and Microsoft planned to fully exit.

PhonePe, the dominant player in digital payments in India with over 650 million registered users, processed nearly 11.4 billion of the country's 25.4 billion Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions in October. Indian business daily The Economic Times on Wednesday first reported PhonePe's plans to resume its IPO. Walmart and PhonePe didn't immediately respond to Reuters' email seeking comment. The Bengaluru-based fintech, which competes with Google Pay and Paytm in India, expects to turn profitable in the next fiscal year, excluding any fee revenue on UPI and government digital payments incentives, according to the person cited above. India bars banks and fintech platforms like PhonePe from charging fees on standard UPI transfers to encourage digital adoption. A government proposal to introduce a 0.4 per cent merchant fee on transactions exceeding 2,000 rupees ($21) was recently deferred indefinitely following opposition from retailers.

FAST

BRUSSELS, Nov 25 : A European Union meeting expected to consider Tesla's bid to win approval for its assisted self-driving system across the bloc has been postponed for Dec. 15, a European Commission spokesperson told Reuters on Wednesday. The Technical Committee for Motor Vehicles (TCMV) had been expected to potentially vote on the system during its December meeting, after no vote was held at two earlier meetings following preliminary approval from the Netherlands in April. The vote is a key hurdle in Tesla's push to bring the technology to Europe. Nearly a dozen countries have followed the Dutch lead, with Italy the most populous to begin a rollout, but EU-wide approval requires support from at least 15 of the bloc's 27 countries representing 65 per cent of its population. The meeting was originally scheduled for Dec. 1, Dutch regulator RDW told Reuters. Belgium's Flanders transport ministry initially said it had been moved to Dec. 7, before the Commission clarified that it would instead take place on Dec. 15.

Source: Reuters

FAST

LONDON, Nov 25 : Online fast-fashion retailer Shein warned on Wednesday that its European business may not recover until the second half of next year after new e-commerce import fees hit sales in its biggest market and dragged down group revenue. Shein's third-quarter results are the first to show the impact of the European Union's €3 ($3.28) fee on e-commerce imports, which has eroded its competitive edge just as the newly listed company seeks to bolster confidence in its business model. Quarterly revenue in Europe fell 27.6 per cent to $2.98 billion after Shein raised prices to offset the additional costs. Group revenue fell 6 per cent to $10.27 billion. CEO Sky Xu said sales in Europe might not recover until the second half of 2027, when most deliveries would be made from European warehouses the company is investing in.

Shein's business model has come under further pressure since the start of November, when the EU began imposing an additional €2 fee on e-commerce parcels. MARKETING SPEND SLASHED Facing a sharp slowdown in sales, Shein cut marketing spending by 41.5 per cent in the quarter, reducing online advertising to protect profitability. Operating income rose 17 per cent from a year earlier to $743 million. Once one of the fastest-growing online retailers, Shein helped intensify price competition for established rivals such as H&M and Zara. But its rapid expansion has stalled since the US and Europe removed duty-free access for e-commerce imports. "Consumers worldwide have become more cautious," the company said in a statement, adding that shoppers are placing more emphasis on value for money. ($1 = 0.9136 euros)

FAST

LONDON, Nov 25 : Retailers heading into the Black Friday shopping period face growing cyber threats as artificial intelligence makes attacks faster and more potent, at a time when the sector has some of the lowest levels of cyber insurance protection. The post-Thanksgiving spree has long represented a lucrative sales opportunity, but more frequent and sophisticated cyberattacks are increasingly testing retailers' cyber resilience. Ransomware attacks on retail, leisure and hospitality businesses are 50 per cent more frequent in November than the monthly average, according to claims data from insurer CFC. Only 43 per cent of small and medium-sized retailers carry cyber insurance, compared with 81 per cent in financial services and 71 per cent in technology. "Retailers spend months making sure their websites, stock and logistics can withstand the surge in customers. But Black Friday should be treated as a resilience exercise as much as a revenue opportunity," said Lindsey Maher, CFC's head of global cyber development.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday bookend one of the retail sector's busiest periods of the year, with consumers searching for deals and retailers often offering hefty discounts. UK shoppers looking to snap up bargains are set to spend £235 ($307) each this Black Friday, with UK spending expected to reach its highest since 2022, research from PwC shows. Retailers don't generally buy additional cyber insurance for a weekend and focus instead on testing and strengthening resilience, said David Molony, Europe, Middle East and Africa head of cyber and financial sponsors at Aon. That matters most at a time of year when revenue depends heavily on technology, he said. "A cyber incident that interrupts the ability to trade during peak season can move very quickly from an operational issue to a material financial loss," he said. US retailer Target incurred net cumulative expenses of $202 million after a 2013 breach during the holiday shopping season that compromised at least 40 million credit cards, the company has said. Complex retail supply chains, copious credit card records and the busy shopping period mean retailers are primed for maximum chaos and interruption, said Sydonie Williams, head of international cyber risks at Beazley. While AI increases the threat risk, it also improves defence mechanisms, she said. Francisco Donoso, chief product and technology officer at Beazley Security, said AI was speeding up attacks and the number of vulnerabilities being exposed was almost six times higher than a year ago. "It's really hard for organisations to keep up," Donoso said. ($1 = 0.7639 pounds)

FAST

LONDON, Nov 25 : Crude oil prices fell on Wednesday as the prospect of a market surplus offset concerns about disruptions to oil exports in the Middle East. Brent crude futures declined 44 cents, or 0.5 per cent, to $90.96 a barrel at 1035 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures slipped 62 cents, or 0.8 per cent, to $81.43 a barrel. Both benchmarks gained more than 2 per cent on Tuesday. "Investors are preoccupied with the thought of supply exceeding demand," said Tamas Varga, an oil analyst at PVM, a brokerage. On Wednesday, Yemen's Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh's financial district. Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, is part of a complex on the kingdom's Gulf coast that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude.

A build-up in crude inventories is also contributing to the softer oil prices, Varga said. US crude stocks rose by 126,000 barrels in the week ended November 20, market sources said on Tuesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Eight analysts polled by Reuters estimated that crude inventories rose by about 1.5 million barrels on average. "Uncertainty about OPEC's 2027 policies in the upcoming November 29 meeting, especially with the UAE no longer restricted by OPEC+ policies and Iraq seeking higher oil output capacity, as well as broader market risk-off are some reasons," said Zhenqiang Seto, a senior research specialist for oil at LSEG. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide on their 2027 output policy. "Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check," said Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute. Attention is also focused on how next year's production quotas will be determined at the OPEC+ meeting, Ueno said. Iraq is pressing OPEC+ to lift its estimate of the country's crude oil production capacity, four people familiar with the matter said, heightening tensions over a review that will help determine how much members can pump next year. Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has also reopened after an "unlawful group" closed a valve on the pipeline, with oil beginning to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya. "However, attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz and exchanges of attacks between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have raised uncertainty over the sustainability of this trend," Ueno said. A container ship was targeted and came to a stop on Tuesday while sailing an "unauthorised" route near the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said, according to state media. On Monday, three vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles as they sailed east through the strait, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Tuesday.

Source: Reuters

FAST

NEW DELHI, Nov 25 : Meta's top executives in India held closed-door talks with the country's opposition Congress party as the two sides try to defuse escalating tensions over the US firm's content moderation practices, four people familiar with the matter said. The talks show how Mark Zuckerberg's company is caught between Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, which has stepped up demands to remove online content it deems illegal, and an opposition accusing it of bias, the latest challenge for Meta in India, its biggest market by users.  Meta's Aman Jain and Natasha Jog, two key executives in India, represented the company at the meeting at Congress headquarters on Tuesday, one person said.  They raised concerns about protests targeting Meta's offices and the depiction of CEO Zuckerberg in posters. Congress raised concerns about a rise in restrictions on its leaders' accounts and posts, and about allegations that Meta favours Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), three other people said. Meta has denied any favouritism.

The meeting marked Meta's first direct engagement with the party since protests by its youth wing began on Friday. The Youth Congress has demanded that Meta restore accounts taken down on government orders and explain how its algorithms restrict posts, and its members have clashed with police near Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram. Congress did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Meta said it moderates content in India in accordance with the law. Meta executives Jain and Jog did not respond. POSTERS TARGETING ZUCKERBERG During the meeting, which lasted more than 40 minutes, Meta said some of the removals were the result of its policy on AI-generated content, one of the people said. Congress countered by citing examples of BJP posts that were also generated using AI but had not been taken down, and told the executives that Meta's takedown policy appeared arbitrary, the person said. Meta made no commitments to the party during the meeting and explained that it was bound by local laws, said a second source. The executives also emphasised that Meta was neutral towards all political parties, the person added. The dispute adds to political pushback for Meta in India, where it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts under local laws in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in all of 2025, company disclosures show. Meta attributes the rise to India's amended IT rules that require faster and more proactive takedowns, but it has triggered a debate over free speech as the government steps up demands to remove online content. The protests took a fresh turn in recent days as posters and banners depicting Zuckerberg in a white shirt, khaki shorts and black cap, the traditional uniform of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), appeared in cities like Delhi, Kolkata, Patna, Mumbai and Bengaluru. The RSS is a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation that is the ideological parent of the BJP. "This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of private companies," BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari wrote on X on Saturday.

Source: Reuters

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 25 : Australia passed a law requiring internet companies to proactively stamp out harmful content and features or face fines of up to 5 per cent of global revenue, a centrepiece of a campaign to rein in Big Tech decried by free speech advocates. The Digital Duty of Care will take effect in a year and replaces a patchwork of online codes of conduct with an all-encompassing law which the government says puts the onus on platforms to prioritise the safety of Australians. It marks another blow for the mostly US-based internet industry, which Australia has accused of undermining its right to regulate products used in the country. In 2025, Australia became the first country to ban under-16s from social media, and the country plans to make large internet companies pay licensing fees for news content, reimbursing the news media. "The Digital Duty of Care is a landmark safety reform in the vein of compulsory seatbelts, plain packaging for cigarettes and gun reform," Communications Minister Anika Wells said in a statement after the law was passed.

"Big Tech can no longer be under any illusions — they are responsible for keeping Australians safe on their platforms, and we will hold them to account if they fail to do so." Companies that breach the law face fines of up to 5 per cent of their global turnover, or A$109 million ($72 million), whichever is greater. Given the larger platforms typically generate annual revenue of hundreds of billions of dollars, the maximum fines could reach tens of billions of dollars. Though tech firms like Meta and YouTube owner Google generally agreed with the government's aim of improving child protection and minimising harmful content, most opposed the bill on the grounds that it gave some discretion to government officials to decide what counts as harmful content. Some industry groups had warned the law might encourage platforms to become heavy-handed when deciding what content to take down as they sought to avoid punishment. The law bans content which "encourages or promotes hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality" and "glorifies crime or encourages dangerous stunts or seriously harmful practices" — classifications some free speech advocates warned could be widely interpreted. "The law remains too vague, leaving businesses unclear on how to comply or how the new rules will make Australians safer," said Jennifer Duxbury, interim managing director of industry group DIGI, which represents internet companies. "The regulator's sweeping powers to use fake accounts and access information about people's use of online services raise serious privacy issues," she added, referring to a part of the law which allows regulators to use anonymous "sock puppet" accounts to investigate platforms for possible wrongdoing. The Australia Institute, a think tank that had campaigned for the law, said its passing was globally significant because it could lead to hefty penalties which "will give social media the incentive they need to clean up their act". ($1 = 1.5165 Australian dollars)

Source: Reuters

BENGALURU, Nov 25 : Cognizant is in talks to take over parts of S&P Global's Capital IQ operations in a deal that could move about 1,500 employees to the IT services provider, two people familiar with the matter said. The proposed transfer covers employees in the data and operations team of the S&P Global unit's India global capability centre (GCC), who would move to Cognizant's payroll under the arrangement, the people said, speaking on condition on anonymity. The discussions are ongoing and the terms could change or the talks could fall apart, the people said. The negotiations come as S&P Global reviews the future of Capital IQ and associated data businesses.

S&P said on October 27 it was exploring strategic alternatives, including a potential separation, for Capital IQ and associated data businesses, which constitute the majority of its Kensho Data & Platforms unit within Market Intelligence. Cognizant has a longstanding relationship with S&P Global and previously performed the services now under discussion before the financial-data provider brought them in-house, one of the people said. S&P Global declined to comment on the potential transaction, saying it does not comment on speculation concerning its "contingent labour partners." Cognizant did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Businesses can use such deals to cut costs and focus on core operations, with AI adding pressure to seek productivity gains and rethink technology and data work, industry experts said. "Moving the India data operations to Cognizant first makes the asset lighter and more sellable and suits the AI/LLM-ready data direction. It is a typical pre-divestiture play," said Phil Fersht, founder of market research firm HFS Research. Gaurav Vasu, founder of market research firm UnearthInsight, said companies typically carve out operations when growth or profitability is under pressure, or when management concludes outsourcing would allow it to focus more on its core business. "They will usually bring in an IT vendor for one specific service or business unit," Vasu said. UnearthInsight estimates the annual "loaded" cost of an employee at an S&P-like global capability centre, including expenses beyond salary, at about $25,000 to $30,000.  On that basis, the cost associated with 1,500 employees would be roughly $38 million to $45 million a year, Vasu said, and would typically be factored into a multi-year services contract. Similar transfers have emerged elsewhere. In October, Best Buy agreed to transition its India GCC to Tata Consultancy Services under a multi-year agreement, with the retailer's India employees moving to TCS. Those deals run alongside a much bigger expansion of global companies' in-house operations in India. India's GCC industry generated $98.4 billion in fiscal 2026, nearly reaching IT industry body Nasscom and consultancy Zinnov's 2030 forecast four years early. The industry's 2,117 centres employed about 2.36 million people.

Nov 24 : Goldman Sachs said strong US data-center power capacity growth is likely to continue through 2028, posing upside risks to power and natural gas demand as the AI boom drives the construction of more, larger and increasingly power-dense facilities. • The brokerage said an additional 52 gigawatts of data-center power capacity could come online in 2028 • "Year-to-date, data-center power capacity and demand have increased by nearly 30 per cent in the US, contributing to more than one third of US total power demand growth," Goldman said in a note dated Tuesday • The rapid expansion could further tighten US power markets and increase natural gas demand, reinforcing Goldman's bullish outlook for Henry Hub gas prices between 2028 and 2030

• The brokerage, however, said potential policy shifts following the midterm elections could moderate the upside risk • "We expect growth acceleration in data centers to be driven not only by a higher volume of facilities, but by increasingly larger physical footprints and higher power density," the note added • Democrats' victories in November's midterm elections, including wins in Republican strongholds and major data center hubs Texas and Georgia, are expected to usher in divided government and could lead to greater scrutiny of data center development

Source: Reuters
